query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for plasma-facing applications in fusion reactors, what single intervention could improve radiation tolerance while preserving mechanical integrity and engineering practicality? Formulate one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the proposed mechanism, predicts a measurable improvement over the unmodified baseline, defines the conditions under which the effect should hold, cites prior evidence supporting the causal rationale, and specifies an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing controlled Ti and carbon during powder metallurgy processing of a tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy to in-situ form uniformly dispersed TiC nanoprecipitates will enhance radiation tolerance by acting as sinks for helium-induced defects while maintaining the alloy’s mechanical integrity and practical manufacturability.
generation.material_initial_state: A tungsten-rich refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., WxTaTiVCr) produced by elemental powder mixing and spark plasma sintering without deliberate optimization for TiC formation.
generation.intervention: Incorporate targeted amounts of Ti and a carbon source during processing to promote the in-situ formation of nanoscale TiC precipitates.
generation.conditions: Under simulated fusion reactor plasma-facing conditions, including elevated temperatures (around 900–1000 °C) and exposure to helium ion irradiation at fluences representative of reactor operation.
generation.structural_mediator: Uniformly dispersed nanoscale TiC precipitates distributed within the grain interiors and along the grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The TiC nanoprecipitates provide defect sinks that capture radiation-induced helium and vacancies, thereby reducing the nucleation and growth of deleterious He bubbles. Simultaneously, these fine precipitates contribute to dispersion strengthening, preserving or even enhancing the alloy’s mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified baseline alloy, the processed alloy with in-situ TiC will show a significantly reduced helium bubble size and density (as measured by TEM) and improved retention of hardness and strength after irradiation.
generation.baseline: The tungsten-based refractory HEA prepared without the deliberate addition of Ti and carbon to promote TiC formation.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected only if the volume fraction and distribution of the TiC precipitates are within an optimal range (e.g., a few weight percent, as previously observed between ~1–8.5%); excessive precipitate formation or inhomogeneous distribution might lead to embrittlement or processing difficulties.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal levels of Ti and carbon addition and the long-term stability of the TiC precipitates under prolonged irradiation require further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of alloy samples: one baseline batch without added Ti/carbon and one with controlled Ti and carbon additions to form in-situ TiC. Subject both batches to helium ion irradiation at reactor-relevant fluences and temperatures (around 1000 °C).
measurements: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to quantify helium bubble size and density
Nanoindentation and tensile testing to determine hardness and strength before and after irradiation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the TiC-containing alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in helium bubble size/density and fails to retain or improve its mechanical properties relative to the baseline after irradiation, then the hypothesis is falsified.

This study presented the microstructures and room-temperature mechanical properties of a HEA (32 Ws) with in-situ TiC prepared by elemental powder mixing followed by spark plasma sintering. The enhanced hardness and strength of the 32 Ws due to distorted lattice and solid solution strengthening were also revealed. Additionally, several W-based alloys were derived from HEA by gradually increasing x up to 90 at.% in xWs. The solid solution strengthening imparted enhanced hardness and strength in W-based alloys as well. The improved hardness and strength of xWs emphasizes the potential of this facile method (i.e., elemental powder mixing) for the development of refractory HEAs. The chemical composition of xWs fulfills the reduced-activation criteria (which are commonly followed for producing reduced-activation steels (Section S1)), , .
